full_text: Kamran Razmavar presents another strange argument, and Jesus did NOT meet Armenians, and in the Bible, there are NO Armenians at all, so ancient Armenia is fabricated. But the existence of countries and peoples is NOT established this way. And now let's debunk this myth about Greater Armenia, which allegedly included Jerusalem. According to Wikipedia, Greater Armenia therefore did not exist in the fourth century, so our era is approximately the fifth. And somewhere in the middle of these 80 years, Jesus Christ was born in Bethlehem, by the way, which is near Jerusalem. Strangely enough, Jesus did NOT meet a single Armenian. There is NOTHING Armenian in the Bible. There is NO great Armenia, there are dozens of state nationalities and NO ethnocentrism. But there are NO Armenians, NO Armenia, and there is NO need to insert it there, it is written 'Mountains of Ararat'. This is a geographical term. The Gospels are NOT a list of all the peoples of the Near East. The absence of a people in the story of Christ's life does NOT mean their absence in history. Moreover, the name Armenia is recorded approximately 5 centuries before the birth of Jesus. Around 520 BC, Darius the First left the Behistun inscription. In the Dri-nepersis text, the country is called 'Armina of the inhabitant of Armenia'. The Encyclopedia Iranica translates the latter as Armenian. Now to Kamran's claim that there is Ararat in the Bible, but there are NO Armenians. Even this is NOT true if we talk about Biblical translations in general. In the classic English translation of the King James Bible, in 2 Kings 19:37 and in the book of Isaiah 37:38, the expression land of Armenia is directly used. In modern translations, in these same places, the land of Ararat is more often used. And this shows the main problem with Kamran's argument. Different linguistic and translation traditions can convey ancient geographical names differently. This is also seen in the Behistun inscription. Ancient Persian versions use the name Armina, while in Velosko-Uras, which means the old Mesopotamian name 'Urartu' that therefore did not exist earlier in the same region. There are independent Greek testimonies. Herodotus from the fifth century BC mentions Armenians. Xenophon in the early 4th century BC repeatedly writes about Armenia and Armenians. Therefore, Kamran's question of why Jesus did NOT meet Armenians historically proves nothing. Persian and Greek sources record Armenia and Armenians a century before 'the birth of Christ'. And the attempt to prove the non-existence of Armenia with the word 'Ararat' collapses on the sources themselves. Kamran simply mixes different linguistic traditions and takes the difference in names for the absence of a country. we will call them erreicht assignates,
